explain.tweet: Before reading Feser’s Five Proofs, learn six words. Potential = what a thing can become. Actual = how it is now. A per se causal series is a stack (cup on desk on floor), not a timeline. “First cause” means non-derivative, not earliest. That one fix answers half the objections.
explain.elevator: Feser’s book argues that God’s existence can be demonstrated by reason alone. But it uses a vocabulary most readers have never met: act and potency, essence and existence, hierarchical causal series, divine simplicity. This module teaches those words first, with everyday examples — cooling coffee, a cup on a desk, a $20 bill — so that when you open the book you are learning the arguments instead of decoding the terms.
explain.twoMinute:
Here is what nobody tells you before you open a book like this.

The arguments are not hard because the logic is hard. They are hard because about eight background ideas get introduced quickly and then used on every page afterwards. Miss one and the next forty pages feel like fog.

The biggest one is this. When most of us hear ‘what caused that?’, we think about the past — what got it started. Feser is almost always asking a different question: what is holding it in being *right now*? And he says there are two completely different kinds of causal chain. One runs backward through time, like a line of ancestors: your grandfather can be dead and the chain still stands. The other is stacked up at this instant, like a coffee cup held by a desk held by a floor held by a foundation held by the earth. In that second kind, every link is borrowing. The desk has no power of its own to keep a cup three feet up — take away the floor and both go down together.

And that is why he says the second kind must have a first member, while the first kind need not. ‘First’ doesn’t mean earliest. It means non-derivative — something with the power built in rather than borrowed. His best image: a paintbrush can’t move itself, and it still couldn’t if the handle were infinitely long. Length isn’t power.

Once you have that, look at what happens to the famous objections. ‘Maybe the universe is infinitely old’ — Feser grants that for the sake of argument; it’s about the other kind of chain. ‘Why can’t the regress be infinite?’ — for linear series, fine; for a stack of borrowers, adding borrowers never produces a lender. ‘Who made God?’ — the arguments never say everything has a cause; they say no *potential* gets actualized without something actual, and the thing they conclude to has no potentials.

The other big one is the word ‘God’. Most debates are two people arguing about different things. The God being defended here isn’t a very powerful being inside the universe. He’s pure actuality — no parts, no change, outside time, the reason anything exists at all. Half the standard objections are aimed at a target this book isn’t defending.

Learn those two things and you can read the book.
explain.eli12:
Imagine a coffee cup sitting on a desk.

Why is the cup up in the air instead of on the ground? The desk is holding it. What holds the desk? The floor. What holds the floor? The foundation of the house. What holds that? The earth.

Now here’s the interesting bit. The desk can’t hold anything up *by itself*. If the floor vanished, the desk would fall and the cup with it. Same for the floor: it only holds the desk because the foundation holds it. Every single one of them is borrowing the ability to hold things up from the thing below.

So ask yourself: could that chain go on forever? Imagine a million desks stacked up, all borrowing. A billion. Infinity of them. Does the cup stay up? No! Because none of them ever had the ability in the first place. They were all just passing along something that has to start somewhere.

Here’s another way to see it. A paintbrush can’t move itself. What if the handle were ten feet long? Still can’t. A mile long? Still can’t. Infinitely long? *Still can’t.* Making the handle longer never turns it into a painter. There has to be somebody holding it.

That is the main idea of this whole book. There are chains of things where everything is borrowing, and those chains have to start with something that isn’t borrowing — something that has the ability built in.

And one more thing. When people argue about God, they usually picture a really, really powerful person somewhere out in space. This book isn’t about that at all. It’s about whatever it is that makes anything exist in the first place — the thing at the bottom that isn’t borrowing from anything.
whiteboard: Draw a stick figure holding a paintbrush. Say: a brush can’t move itself. Now draw the handle running off the edge of the board. Say: make it infinitely long — still can’t move itself. Length isn’t power. That single picture is the heart of the book.

Draw two columns. Head the left ‘THEN’ and the right ‘NOW’. Under THEN, draw grandfather → father → son. Under NOW, draw a cup on a desk on a floor on the earth. Say: these are the two kinds of causal chain, and everything depends on telling them apart.

Under THEN write: ‘each keeps its power — grandfather can be dead.’ Under NOW write: ‘each borrows, right now — remove the floor and everything falls.’ Circle the NOW column. Say: the whole book is about this column.
Write ‘FIRST ≠ EARLIEST’ in large letters and box it. Say: first means the one with power built in. Not the starting gun. Draw an arrow from the box to the earth at the bottom of the NOW stack.

Draw a coffee cup and write beside it ACTUAL: hot, liquid, in a cup. Underneath write POTENTIAL: cold, spilled, a stain. Then write in a different colour: NOT chicken soup, NOT a chicken. Say: a potential is real but limited, which is why it isn’t the same as nothing.

Write the principle of causality in full: ‘No potential is actualized unless something already actual actualizes it.’ Then cross out, beneath it, ‘everything has a cause.’ Say: that second sentence is the one everybody attacks, and nobody in this book says it.

Draw two circles side by side. Label one ‘a very powerful being’ and put it inside a big box labelled ‘the universe’. Label the other ‘pure actuality’ and draw it outside the box, with arrows pointing into the box. Say: most arguments about God are two people pointing at different circles.

Write three sentences in a column: ‘Fido is a dog / Rover is a dog’ — label it UNIVOCAL. ‘A bat flew / I swung the bat’ — label it EQUIVOCAL. ‘Good wine / good man’ — label it ANALOGICAL. Say: God-talk is the third one, and it is literal, not metaphor.

Draw a bookshelf with a book on it, floating with nothing underneath. Write ‘brute fact?’ with an arrow to the shelf. Say: if the shelf has no tendency to stay up, it can’t give the book one. That’s the argument against stopping at an unexplained fact.

Finish by writing the four-part structure of every chapter: 1 informal Stage 1 / 2 informal Stage 2 / 3 formal numbered steps / 4 objections. Say: the numbered list is always a recap. You have already read it in prose.
explain.keyAnalogy: The infinitely long paintbrush. Use it the moment anyone says ‘why can’t the causes just go back forever?’ — and use it physically: hold an imaginary brush, then keep backing away as the handle grows. Ask at each stage, ‘has it started painting yet?’ The listener will laugh, and the laugh is the understanding arriving. Then make the point explicit: adding length adds more of something that has no power of its own, and no amount of that ever adds up to power. Finish by naming the target: this is why the age of the universe is irrelevant to the argument. A beginningless universe is just a very long handle.

persuade.coreInsight:
**The insight:** there are two kinds of causal chain, and almost everyone has only ever thought about one of them.

The kind we all know runs backward through time and each link keeps its power once it has it. Your grandfather caused your father, who caused you, and your grandfather can be long dead. You pressed a button, the air conditioner came on, and it goes on cooling after you leave the house. Asking whether such a chain has a beginning is a reasonable question with no obvious answer, which is why people who have only this picture in mind hear ‘first cause’ as ‘the event at the very start’.

The other kind is stacked up at this instant, and every link is borrowing. The cup is three feet up because the desk holds it; the desk holds it only because the floor holds the desk; the floor only because the foundation. Nothing in the stack has any power of its own. And that changes everything about the regress question: adding more borrowers never produces a lender, so this kind of chain must terminate in something with power built in — which is what ‘first’ means here, not ‘earliest’.

**Why it usually fails to click.** Two reasons, and both are about the listener’s mental picture rather than their intelligence. First, the word ‘cause’ carries three centuries of habit pointing at the past; every time your listener hears ‘cause’ they will picture a timeline, and the whole argument will sound like an argument about the Big Bang. Second, the examples that make the second kind vivid — cup, desk, floor — sound so trivial that people assume they must be missing something deep, when in fact the triviality is the point: it is a structure you can see on your own desk.

**What to do about it.** Do not argue. Build the picture. Put an object on a table and ask what is holding it up, and keep asking. Only when your listener has the stack in their head should you introduce the word ‘first’, and then define it immediately: not earliest, but non-derivative. If you introduce the conclusion before the picture, they will fit it into the timeline they already have, and you will spend the rest of the conversation talking past each other.

audiences.startingPoint: Believes that physics is steadily explaining everything that needs explaining, that appeals to God are always appeals to gaps, and that metaphysics is what people did before they had instruments.
audiences.approach: Concede more than they expect. Grant the Big Bang, grant an eternal or cyclic multiverse, grant that every gap you can name will eventually close. Then point out that you have granted all of that and the question has not been touched, because the question is not how things work but why anything is there to work at all. Use the layered-laws point from chapter 7: if law C holds because of law B, and B because of A, you have a hierarchical series, and stopping at A as a brute fact does not explain B and C but cancels the explanation — because if A has no tendency of its own, it has nothing to impart.
audiences.openingQuestion: Suppose physics finishes tomorrow — a complete final theory, every constant derived, no gaps. Would that tell us why there is a universe for the theory to be about?
audiences.avoid: Never cite a scientific mystery as evidence. The moment you say ‘science can’t explain consciousness / the fine-tuning / the origin of life’, you have turned your argument into exactly the god-of-the-gaps argument they were expecting, and you will deserve the response you get.

audiences.startingPoint: Was taught a God who is a very powerful person in the sky, found that picture incoherent or unworthy, and left. Often carries real hurt and expects to be argued at.
audiences.approach: Agree with the rejection before offering anything. The God they left — a being inside the universe, subject to the same questions as everything in it — is one classical theism also denies, and saying so plainly is both true and disarming. Then be explicit that you are not asking them to come back to anything; you are asking whether the arguments about pure actuality are sound, which is a different question from what any institution taught them.
audiences.openingQuestion: When you stopped believing, what exactly was it that you stopped believing in? I ask because the thing Feser is defending may not be the same thing.
audiences.avoid: Do not treat the conversation as a recovery operation, and do not imply their leaving was a failure of reasoning. If they sense you are managing them rather than thinking with them, the conversation is over and you will not be told.

audiences.startingPoint: Not hostile, just unconvinced that any of this matters. Suspects philosophy is a word game that never resolves, and has limited patience for anything without a payoff.
audiences.approach: Do not start with God at all. Start with the skill: most arguments people find persuasive have a premise nobody stated, and learning to find it is useful in every part of life. Reconstruct something from the news — a policy claim, an ad — and show the hidden premise. Only then note that the same technique applied to the biggest question anyone has asked is what this book is. The payoff you are selling is clarity, not conversion.
audiences.openingQuestion: Want to see a trick? Give me any confident opinion you heard this week and I’ll find the assumption underneath it in about a minute.
audiences.avoid: Do not oversell the stakes or use the phrase ‘the most important question you’ll ever face’. Pressure reads as sales, and this listener is unusually good at detecting sales.

audiences.who: The believer who has never seen an argument
audiences.startingPoint: Believes on the basis of upbringing, community and experience; has no idea that arguments of this kind exist; may be slightly anxious that examining the question is disloyal.
audiences.approach: Distinguish natural theology from faith at the outset and treat the distinction as good news rather than a threat: the tradition has held for two thousand years that reason can reach this far on its own. Then go slowly through act and potency, because this reader often has to unlearn a personalist picture of God that the arguments will not support. Expect the classical attributes — timelessness, simplicity, immutability — to feel cold at first, and say so before they do.
audiences.openingQuestion: If someone asked you tonight why you believe God exists, and ‘because I was raised that way’ were off the table, what would you say?
audiences.avoid: Do not disparage the personalist picture as childish. It is how nearly everyone starts, including most of the tradition’s greatest figures, and mocking it makes the classical account feel like a loss rather than a discovery.

audiences.who: The analytically trained philosopher or philosophy student
audiences.startingPoint: Knows validity, soundness, modality and possible worlds; probably learned that cosmological arguments were dispatched by Hume and Kant; may regard Aristotelian metaphysics as a museum piece.
audiences.approach: Skip the hand-holding entirely and go straight to the disputed premises. Be precise about what Feser is and is not claiming: not ‘everything has a cause’, not an inference to the best explanation, not a design argument. The most productive opening is usually the difference between per se and per accidens series, followed by the question of whether the standard textbook ‘basic cosmological argument’ is a straw man — Feser argues in chapter 7 that it is, with a long pedigree running through Hume and Russell.
audiences.openingQuestion: Which premise of the argument from change do you actually reject — the principle of causality, or the impossibility of an infinite essentially ordered series?
audiences.avoid: Do not use the beginner analogies. Cup-and-desk with this audience reads as condescension, and you will lose the exchange on tone before you reach the substance.

audiences.startingPoint: Has read Dawkins or Hitchens, is confident the arguments for God are feeble, and has a set of one-line replies ready: who made God, one god further, god of the gaps, Ockham’s razor.
audiences.approach: Take the one-liners seriously and answer them one at a time, because each has a precise answer and answering them is the fastest route to credibility. ‘Who made God’ attacks a premise nobody holds. ‘One god further’ conflates a being inside the universe with the source of existence. ‘God of the gaps’ misses that the argument concerns features anything whatever must have. Then make the honest offer: you are not asking them to agree, only to attack the argument that is actually on the page.
audiences.openingQuestion: Before we start — can you state the version of the cosmological argument you think fails? I want to make sure we’re talking about the same argument.
audiences.avoid: Do not match their register. Feser himself calls some of these objections staggeringly feeble, and he has earned that after three hundred pages; borrowing the tone without the argument just produces a shouting match.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: So you’re reading a book that claims to *prove* God exists. Isn’t that a bit much? Nobody proves anything about God.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: That is the claim, and I was surprised by how strong it is. Not ‘God probably exists’ or ‘God is the best explanation’ — he says these are demonstrations, like proofs in geometry. Valid arguments from premises he says are certain.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Then it’s easy. Everything has a cause, God is the exception, therefore God. That argument is two thousand years old and it was dead on arrival. Who made God?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Genuinely, that’s not the argument. No premise in the book says everything has a cause. The principle is narrower: no potential gets actualized unless something already actual actualizes it.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: That sounds like the same thing in fancier words.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It isn’t, and here is the difference. ‘Everything has a cause’ applies to everything, so God would be a plain exception and you’d be right to object. The actual principle applies to potentials being actualized. Something with no potentials isn’t exempted from the rule — the rule has nothing to say about it.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Convenient. You define your conclusion so the rule can’t reach it.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It would be, if it were a definition. It’s a conclusion, and it takes fifty steps to get there. And the arguments say *why* other things need causes: they’re mixtures of what they are and what they could be. Whatever has no unrealized potentials couldn’t have a cause even in principle — there’s nothing there to be actualized.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Fine. But why does the chain need to stop? Why not causes all the way back? The universe might be infinitely old — plenty of cosmologists think so.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Feser grants that. Explicitly, for the sake of argument — eternal universe, multiverse, no beginning. It doesn’t affect the argument, because he isn’t arguing about that kind of chain.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: There’s another kind?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Look at your coffee. It’s off the ground because the table holds it. The table stays up because the floor does. The floor because the foundation, the foundation because the earth. Now notice: none of them has any power of its own. Take away the floor, and the table and the cup go down together — instantly, not eventually.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Sure. So?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: So compare it to your ancestors. Your grandfather caused your father, who caused you — and your grandfather can be dead. That chain doesn’t need him around any more. But the table needs the floor *right now*. Everything in the stack is borrowing.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: I see the difference. But I still don’t see why the stack can’t be infinite.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Try it. A paintbrush can’t move itself. Make the handle ten feet long — still can’t. A mile. Infinitely long. Has it started painting?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Right. Length isn’t power. Everything in that stack is a borrower, and adding borrowers never produces a lender. That’s the actual claim: not that infinite series are impossible, but that a series in which nothing has power of its own explains nothing, however long.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: All right, that’s better than I expected. But suppose I grant it. You get to something at the bottom. Why call that God? Why not a quantum field, or just the way things are?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: That’s the best objection you’ve made, and the book spends a whole stage of every chapter on it. The short version: a quantum field is one physical thing among others — it has states, it could have been otherwise, it has parts. So it’s a candidate for a member of the stack, not for the thing the stack rests on.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: And you get from ‘not a quantum field’ to ‘a god who cares what I do on weekends’ how, exactly?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Step by step, and each step is attackable. If it were material it would have unrealized potentials — so immaterial. If it were in time it would change — so timeless. There can’t be two, because you’d need something to tell them apart and each would then be ‘pure actuality plus something extra’. All causal power derives from it, which is what omnipotence means.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: That’s a lot of weight on ‘no unrealized potentials’.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It is. That’s exactly where I’d push if I wanted to break the argument, and I’d say so to Feser’s face. What I’d stop doing is asking who made God — that one really is aimed at a position nobody in the book holds.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Here’s my honest worry. This all feels like a machine for reaching a conclusion you already wanted.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It might be. But notice that worry is about me, not about step 12. And it cuts both ways — you don’t want the conclusion either. The only way out for either of us is to look at the premises. Which one do you actually reject?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Probably that a thing’s existing right now needs something actualizing it. Why can’t things just keep existing?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Now we’re in the right room — that’s called existential inertia, and it's one of the live debates. Chapter 1 argues against it and chapter 4 comes at it from another direction. I don’t think I can settle it for you at this table, and I’d rather admit that than bluff.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: That’s the most honest thing anyone has said to me about this.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It’s also the fastest way to find out whether the argument works. Read chapter 1 and tell me where it breaks. If you find it, I want to know.

socratic: Put your coffee on the table. What is holding it up? And what is holding that up? Keep going — where does it stop, and what would have to be true of the last thing?
If I remove the floor, when does the table fall? Now compare: if your grandfather had died before you were born, would you cease to exist? What’s different about those two cases?
A paintbrush can’t move itself. If the handle were infinitely long, could it? What exactly does length add — and what does it fail to add?
When you ask what caused your coffee, do you mean what made it twenty minutes ago, or what keeps it in existence right now? Are those the same question? Could they have different answers?

Here is hot coffee. Can it become cold? Can it become chicken soup? Can it become a live chicken? If one of those is different from the others, what does that tell you about whether ‘potential’ is just another word for nothing?
Suppose I say the book stays up because of the shelf, and the shelf stays up for no reason whatsoever — it just does, brute fact. Have I explained why the book is up there?
You know exactly what a unicorn is. Does that tell you whether any exist? What about a lion — did knowing what a lion is tell you that there are lions?
Before there were any human beings, was seven a prime number? If so, where was that truth, and what was it a truth about?
Is ‘good’ doing the same job in ‘good wine’ and ‘good man’? Is it doing a completely unrelated job, the way ‘bat’ does in two sentences? If neither — what is the third option?
You don’t believe in Zeus. What kind of thing would Zeus have been — something inside the universe, or the reason there is a universe? Does rejecting the first commit you to rejecting the second?
Suppose an argument is valid and you dislike the conclusion. What are your options? Now name every option that doesn’t involve finding a false premise.
If two intelligent people disagree about something for two thousand years, does that show neither has a proof? Would you say the same about the interpretation of quantum mechanics?
Can you picture the number seventeen? Can you reason about it correctly? What does that suggest about whether ‘I can’t picture it’ is a good objection to anything?
You’d agree a cause can’t give what it doesn’t have. Does that mean a boy needs a black eye to give one? What has to be true instead?

traps.trap: Using the word ‘cause’ without specifying which kind, so your listener silently imports the past-tense picture and hears the whole thing as an argument about the Big Bang.
traps.fix: Say ‘holding it in being right now’ before you ever say ‘cause’. Build the stack picture first; introduce the vocabulary only after they can see it.

traps.trap: Saying ‘first cause’ and leaving it undefined, so the listener pictures a starting gun.
traps.fix: Never say ‘first’ without immediately adding ‘meaning it has the power built in, not that it came earliest’. Every single time, until it becomes reflex.

traps.trap: Letting the conversation become about the age of the universe.
traps.fix: Concede it loudly and early: grant an eternal universe, a multiverse, no beginning at all. Then show that the question is untouched. Conceding is more persuasive than contesting, and it is what Feser himself does.

traps.trap: Reaching for a scientific mystery — consciousness, fine-tuning, the origin of life — as supporting evidence.
traps.fix: Don’t. You have just built a god-of-the-gaps argument on your own initiative. The whole point is that these arguments concern features anything whatever must have, not phenomena awaiting explanation.

traps.trap: Defending a God your listener already rejects — a very powerful person somewhere, with a location and a history.
traps.fix: Find out what they mean by the word in the first two minutes, and say plainly which picture you are and are not defending. Often you will find you agree with their rejection.

traps.trap: Presenting the fifty-step argument, or any long chain of steps, in conversation.
traps.fix: Nobody has ever been persuaded by a numbered list spoken aloud. Give one picture — the paintbrush — and one question, and let them do the work. Save the steps for when they ask.

traps.trap: Bluffing past a question you can’t answer because you’re afraid of losing the exchange.
traps.fix: Say ‘I don’t know, that’s in chapter 5 and I haven’t worked it through’. It costs you nothing and buys enormous credibility — and the honest version of the conversation is the only one that can actually change anyone’s mind.

traps.trap: Treating every objection as an attack to be repelled, so the exchange becomes a contest.
traps.fix: Grade objections out loud: ‘that one’s a straw man, but the one you asked before it is serious and here’s where the book takes it up’. Conceding the good ones makes your resistance to the bad ones mean something.

traps.trap: Using the beginner analogies with someone who has philosophical training.
traps.fix: Read the room. With a trained listener, name the premises and ask which they reject; cup-and-desk will read as condescension and you will lose on tone before you reach the substance.

teachBack:
**The challenge.** Explain the difference between a linear and a hierarchical causal series to a real human being who has never studied philosophy — a friend, a sibling, a colleague at lunch — in under five minutes, using nothing but objects within arm’s reach.

**The constraints, and they matter.**

- No jargon at all. You may not say *per se*, *per accidens*, *actualize*, *potency*, *contingent*, or *metaphysics*. If you need a technical word, define it in ordinary language first and then use the ordinary version.
- You must use a physical object they can see. Put something on a table and work from there.
- You must get them to say out loud why the stack needs something with power of its own. If you say it for them, you have failed the exercise.
- You may not mention God. This is an exercise about causal structure, and smuggling in the conclusion will make your listener defensive and teach you nothing about whether the explanation worked.

**How to check yourself.** Afterwards, ask them two questions. First: ‘give me your own example of each kind of chain.’ If the examples are good, the idea landed; if they hand back your cup and desk, it didn’t. Second: ‘if the stack had a million things in it instead of four, would that change anything?’ If they say no and can say why, you have taught it. If they hesitate, go back to the paintbrush.

**The harder version, once you can do the first.** Same exercise, but your listener is allowed to interrupt with the three standard objections — ‘maybe it’s infinite’, ‘maybe the universe is eternal’, ‘who holds up the last thing’ — and you must answer each without notes and without raising your voice.

**A written version, if no victim is available.** Write two paragraphs. The first explains the distinction to a curious twelve-year-old. The second explains it to someone with a physics degree who suspects this is medieval nonsense. Then compare them: the second should not be longer or more technical, only differently addressed. If you needed more jargon for the physicist, you probably don’t understand it yet.

**Why this particular challenge.** Feser’s five arguments diverge in their starting points and converge in their conclusion, and of everything in this primer, this one distinction is doing the most work in the most chapters. If you can teach it cold, chapter 1 will read like a summary of things you already know — which is exactly the state you want to be in on page 17.
videoPrompt:
Audience: an adult who has never taken a philosophy class and is about to read Edward Feser’s *Five Proofs of the Existence of God* for the first time. They are curious and intelligent but have no background at all, and they are slightly intimidated. Tone: warm, patient, unhurried, concrete — a good tutor at a kitchen table, never a lecturer. Do not argue for or against God’s existence; this is orientation, not persuasion.

Cover the ideas in this order and give each one time: (1) what philosophy and natural theology are, and how natural theology differs from faith and from science; (2) how to find the premises and conclusion inside ordinary prose, and what validity and soundness mean; (3) actuality and potentiality, using the cooling coffee — stressing that coffee can become cold but not chicken soup; (4) the difference between a linear chain of causes running back through time and a hierarchical stack of causes operating right now, using the cup on the desk on the floor, and the infinitely long paintbrush. Spend the most time here: it is the single most important idea. (5) essence versus existence, using lions, pterodactyls and unicorns; (6) what classical theism means — pure actuality, simplicity, timelessness — as against a very powerful being inside the universe.

Correct these misconceptions explicitly: that the arguments assume ‘everything has a cause’; that ‘first cause’ means earliest in time; that the arguments depend on the universe having had a beginning; and that ‘simple’ means easy to understand. End by describing the four-part shape of every proof chapter — informal stage 1, informal stage 2, formal numbered steps, objections — and reassuring the listener that a fifty-step argument is always a recap of pages they will already have read.
